### 2026-10-07: Oct 7th, Starting the Starboy!!

**4h**

Oct 7th, Starting the Starboy!!

Today, I finally started building my first pcb, a personalized Starboy! The goal for today was to download KiCad and start figuring out how I wanted the project to actually work. I've done a little bit of work using breadboards and circuits before but I had never designed a pcb so I was pretty excited.

After downloading Kicad, I downloaded the starter package and installed all the symbol and footprint libraries. I placed all the components into my schematic after researching what they did and how they worked.
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/102f1d0f854c9356fa8be332c8b8d2c5b7e226d4eac662ac7ca1176b1cb6701a.png)

After that I started making all the GND, +3.3V and  connections together . I was able to figure out the general UI of KiCad but got stuck trying to figure out how to assign values to my resistors. Luckily I found a KiCad forum post that had the right solution: https://forum.kicad.info/t/new-user-cant-figure-out-how-to-add-values-to-resistors/48332. Once I figured that out, I finished up wiring all the connections.

After finishing the schematic, I moved on to assigning footprints to all my components.
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/2f612e5ee121e5497faf8bfb2d95823798437ffb1672036708852428eef85861.png)
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/9a447896775ab9fb6c199ce1684c2b8a23f364ce90fe52390dd9f8fbec16bd83.png)

I ran into some issues here because I didn't really understand how footprint assignment worked. After a quick YouTube tutorial, I managed to get through it, only to immediately run into another error. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y8-tcDHaVlU

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/397c1cab6a0d71aaf04ad42ba92dcb50e5ae4614a5cfcd2863ebdea744bb0f22.png)

A quick google search showed me the error was because This error occurs because of a footprint mismatch in KiCad. Your schematic symbol for U1 has at least 22 pins, but the assigned PCB footprint (Sensor:Aosong_DHT11_5.5x12.0_P2.54mm) only has 4 physical pads (typically pins 1, 2, 3, and 4 for a DHT11 sensor).

A quick Google search showed me that the error was caused by a footprint mismatch in KiCad. Basically, my schematic symbol for U1 had at least 22 pins, while the footprint I had assigned to it, Sensor:Aosong_DHT11_5.5x12.0_P2.54mm, only had 4 physical pads. Since they didn't match, I deleted my ESP32 this time renaming it to U2 to follow the guide more closely and after redoing the connections, I got it to work and had my physical pcb ready to be started.
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/45782a23b2bc006f3f2e92f716490368a2ede17e9252ad2b8868bb2f8b7f508e.png)

The tl;dr is that I got the Starboy project set up, researched the components I used, did all the connections, added all the footprints, redid my connections  and eventually finished the schematic.

Next time, I'm going to start designing the actual pcb, and customizing it with special touches and a cool theme so its unique to me.

### 2026-10-11: # Oct 11th, Last Day for Starbie!

**4h**

# Oct 11th, Last Day for Starbie!

Today was the last day to finish and submit my Starbie project. After finishing my schematic, and PCB board on KiCad all that was left was to finish the code on Arduino as well as build the entire repo including uploading all the files and writing the readme. Admittedly, I had procrastinated forcing me to grind out 5 hours today to finish.

______
### Firmware
I began with my arduino code. I took the base code and made minor changes including changing the starting values for my pet's starting joy, energy and fullness so I wouldn't have to constantly feed it. After that, I added a special sparkle trail for my pet. The last change I did to the original Starbie.ino file was to draw my own bitmap pet. I took this black and white image of the hollow knight and using image2cpp turned it into Arduino bit array.
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/b17f7a2728fce0f60e8f95966007796fe4a7964baf8c21cc950128c299b4c139.png)

When building this new bitmap pet, I had to round off its width and heigh to 240 x 336 to keep things simpler and allow the image to be divided by 8. After taking the array, I pasted it into my code, where it doubled the total lines of the file, before adjusting the corresponding bitmap pet values. With that the firmware was done, and I tested it where it successfully compiled.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/6334b7f82eccc1757267165b9f77fcd5376602a42384774e97efc01286aa459b.png)
____
Finally, I had finished the three parts to my project, the schematic, the board and now the firmware.  All that was left to do now was build the entire project repo which meant uploading all the files, writing the readme and getting the bom.csv from kicad.
---
 Getting the BOM.CSV

At first, I didn't know what BOM stood for so after a bit of searching, I managed to find out it stood for Bill of Materials. from there I had to search online for how to generate the BOM off Kicad, Upload it to github and then sync it to my halflife page. I went onto my schematic, and exported the BOM as a csv file under the tools menu before dropping the file into github.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/d34def793a82601e897e059a1e341d3949a18677f2af1aba39cdbcada5eaab51.png)

----
Uploading all the files

For the files I had 2 files that were automatically done by halflife including the journal md file and the BOM file which was blank. From there I uploaded the kicad sch file for the schematic and the kicad_pro file for the board itself.  I also downloading the gerbers and drill files, zipped them together to push them to the repo. Finally, I uploaded my edited version of the Starbie.ino file.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/a75fb5e43f1c886f32d8c26996a3090316da136045475f0b2dc887e33703956b.png)

----
Writing the Readme

For the readme, I wanted to document the entire build process, from creating the schematic in KiCad to designing the actual PCB and modifying the code.

I went through the different stages of the project and explained what I did in each one. I also wrote about some of the challenges I ran into, like figuring out how to assign footprints and troubleshooting the errors in my schematic. Since this was my first time designing a PCB, I wanted to include what I learned along the way too.

After that, I organized everything into sections so it would be easy for someone else to understand how the project was built. I covered the schematic, PCB layout, code and firmware, and what I learned throughout the process.

Tldr: Finished the firmware, built the project repo including BOM and ReadMe

Next thing to do: Submit the project

### 2026-10-25: # KeySync — Final Revisions and Approval Feedback

**5h**

# KeySync — Final Revisions and Approval Feedback
October 25-27, 2026

For the last few days I focused on addressing the feedback I received before my KeySync project could be approved. There were several things that needed improvement, including the editable PCB files, firmware display dimensions, component list, PCB routing, and documentation. My goal was to make the project more accurate, complete, and easier for someone else to understand and reproduce.

### Fixing the Firmware and Bitmap Pet

The first issue was that my firmware was configured for a 236 × 336 display, even though my OLED module only supports 128 × 64 pixels. This meant that the display dimensions and pet bitmap needed to be corrected. I updated the screen dimensions in the firmware by reassigning the variables as 124 for the length by 64 pixels for the width. I also replaced the oversized bitmap with a smaller 32 × 32 pixel pet sprite. Since each row of a 32-pixel-wide bitmap requires four bytes, the new sprite only needed 128 bytes of bitmap data. This made the pet suitable for the actual display resolution and reduced the amount of data the firmware needed to store.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/d5ba0bb6c270e8f4a5e3ae5931e0a02c0dfff81ee232d46299ea4e8028362dd9.png)
This is a photo of the adjusted 32x32 pixel bitmap pet.

### Revising the PCB Layout

I also revisited my PCB design in KiCad and redid the routing on the B.Cu copper layer. When building Starbie, I didn't know we could actually use the B.Cu layer so I undid all my messing routing on the F.Cu layer and then I was  needed to make sure the traces were properly routed and that the board layout was consistent with the circuit connections.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/f0e2f20bc77750a5fa904156d4bf096ebb9857c9bc8014bf030917fbdf6dd90d.png)

### Fixing the Bill of Materials

Another important change was correcting the BOM so that it represented the actual physical components required to build KeySync. Previously, I realized I forgot to change some of the entries which were just headers instead of the actual components that they were connect to. I updated the list to identify the actual OLED display and MPU6050 sensor modules. I also included the PCB, resistor, and keycaps, making the BOM more representative of the complete project. This made the parts list more useful for estimating costs, sourcing components, and reproducing the build.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/c19cbf0153217356e5f93b75acc4312e1d7b716141ff6b9301a24c8495798cc0.png)

### Updating the GitHub Repository and README

Finally, I spent time reorganizing my GitHub repository to make the project files easier to navigate and ensure that everything needed for Starbie was included. During my previous upload, I had forgotten to include the Gerber fabrication files, so I made sure to add the Gerber ZIP this time alongside the editable KiCad PCB, schematic, and project files. I also reviewed the other files in the repository, including the firmware, BOM, and journal, to make the repository more complete and ensure that the actual design files were available rather than just the finished manufacturing outputs.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/9add44d56b0d1ec69f98909a6b713e5734230cd3a468a150f599e20b370aa60d.png)

I then updated the README to better explain the project and how to use it. I added a properly formatted BOM table listing the required components, quantities, and relevant purchasing information, including the actual OLED and MPU6050 modules, the PCB, resistor, and keycaps. This makes it easier for someone to identify the parts needed to build KeySync and understand the project's hardware costs. I also added a controls section explaining how to interact with the MIDI controller, so readers can understand its functionality without having to dig through the firmware.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/b23b294a14436bb86307cfed3c1a3c599fd4568ac9c83499759c1a282d159fbc.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/71e93d8426cef7c811a3e811ffedffba94eb6caecedb1f8521cf6b7d764142b2.png)
